lead: A power screw turns rotation into straight-line motion: turning the screw pushes a nut, or the screw itself, along its axis. The thread is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder, so the torque must lift the load up that slope and beat friction on it. A small lead angle gives a large force for a small torque and makes the screw hold its load when let go. Screw jacks, vices, lathe lead screws, presses and valve spindles all work this way.
prereq: You need friction on an inclined plane, and combined direct and torsional stress from the chapters on stresses.

sections.h3: Thread forms and the inclined plane

blocks.text: Square threads have the highest efficiency but are hard to cut. ISO trapezoidal threads (30° included angle) and Acme threads (29°) are easier to make and can take up wear with a split nut. Buttress threads carry heavy load in one direction only.

For a square thread of nominal diameter d and pitch p, the core diameter is d<sub>c</sub> = d − p and the mean diameter d<sub>m</sub> = d − p/2. Unwrap one turn at the mean diameter: it becomes a slope of base πd<sub>m</sub> and height l, the lead (l = p for one start, 2p for two starts).

blocks.where: α is the lead (helix) angle. The friction angle φ is given by tan φ = μ, the thread friction coefficient.
T<sub>r</sub> is the torque to raise load W in N·mm. In terms of μ: T<sub>r</sub> = (Wd<sub>m</sub>/2)(μ + tan α)/(1 − μ tan α).
T<sub>l</sub> is the torque to lower the load, (Wd<sub>m</sub>/2)(μ − tan α)/(1 + μ tan α).

blocks.text: If φ > α, Tl is positive: a torque must be applied to lower the load, so the screw holds the load by itself. It is self-locking. If φ < α, Tl is negative and the load runs the screw down: it overhauls.

A thrust collar between the rotating screw and the load cup adds friction torque Tc = μc·W·Rm, where Rm = (R₁ + R₂)/2 is the mean collar radius (uniform wear). Tc is added both when raising and when lowering, so a collar makes a screw harder to overhaul.

blocks.where: η is the efficiency; W·l is the work done on the load in one turn; 2πT the work put in. For a square thread without a collar, η = tan α/tan(α + φ).

blocks.text: A self-locking square-thread screw has an efficiency below 50 %: putting φ = α in tan α/tan(2α) gives (1 − tan²α)/2, which is under ½. For a trapezoidal or Acme thread, use μ/cos 15° (or μ/cos 14.5°) in place of μ, because the inclined flanks press harder on the nut.

sections.h3: Stresses in the screw and the nut

items: Direct stress on the core: σ<sub>c</sub> = W/(πd<sub>c</sub>²/4).
Torsional shear on the core: τ = 16T/(πd<sub>c</sub>³).

Bearing pressure on the threads: p<sub>b</sub> = W/(πd<sub>m</sub>·h·z), with h = p/2 the thread depth and z the number of threads in the nut. Tables give the permissible pressure for each pair of materials; it falls as the rubbing speed rises.
Thread shear: τ = W/(πd<sub>c</sub>·(p/2)·z) on the screw and W/(πd·(p/2)·z) on the nut.
A long screw in compression must also be checked for buckling (Euler or Johnson).

examples.question: A single-start square-thread screw has d<sub>m</sub> = 24 mm and lead 6 mm. It raises W = 20 kN with μ = 0.15. Find α, the raising and lowering torques and the efficiency, and say whether it self-locks. Then add a collar with μ<sub>c</sub> = 0.12 and R<sub>m</sub> = 20 mm.
steps: T<sub>l</sub> = 240 000 × (0.15 − 0.0796)/(1 + 0.15 × 0.0796) = 16 700 N·mm. Positive, so φ > α and the screw self-locks.
examples.answer: α = 4.55°, T<sub>r</sub> = 55.8 N·m, T<sub>l</sub> = 16.7 N·m, η = 34.2 %, self-locking; with the collar, 103.8 N·m and 18.4 %.

examples.question: A screw jack lifts 50 kN with a single-start square thread 50 mm × 8 mm. Thread and collar friction are both μ = 0.12; the collar has outer and inner radii 40 mm and 20 mm. Find the torque, efficiency, core stresses and the number of threads in the nut for a bearing pressure of 18 MPa.
steps: Collar: R<sub>m</sub> = 30 mm, T<sub>c</sub> = 0.12 × 50 000 × 30 = 180 000 N·mm. Total T = 383 000 N·mm = 383 N·m.
Nut: z = 50 000/(π × 46 × 4 × 18) = 4.8, so z = 5 threads and nut height 5 × 8 = 40 mm (p<sub>b</sub> = 17.3 MPa).
Thread shear with z = 5: screw 50 000/(π × 42 × 4 × 5) = 18.9 MPa, nut 50 000/(π × 50 × 4 × 5) = 15.9 MPa.
examples.answer: T = 383 N·m, η = 16.6 %, τ<sub>max</sub> = 22.8 MPa, nut of 5 threads (40 mm); a handle 1 m long needs about 383 N of push.

traps: Using the nominal d in tan α and in the torque. Both use the mean diameter d<sub>m</sub> = d − p/2.
Using pitch for lead on a multi-start screw. A two-start thread has l = 2p, which doubles tan α.
Reading T<sub>l</sub> ≤ 0 as self-locking. A negative lowering torque means the load drives the screw down; self-locking needs T<sub>l</sub> > 0, that is φ > α.
Leaving out collar friction. In the screw jack it is 180 of the 383 N·m, almost half.
Using μ for a trapezoidal thread. Use μ/cos 15°.

quiz.q: State the conditions for a square-thread screw to be self-locking and to overhaul.
quiz.a: Self-locking when φ > α (μ > tan α); overhauling when φ < α.

quiz.q: Why is the efficiency of a self-locking screw always below 50 %?
quiz.a: η = tan α/tan(α + φ). The largest α that still self-locks is α = φ, which gives tan α/tan 2α = (1 − tan²α)/2, less than 0.5.

quiz.q: Why are trapezoidal threads used in lathe lead screws although square threads are more efficient?
quiz.a: They are easier to cut and stronger at the root, and a split nut can close on the sloping flanks to take up wear and backlash.

quiz.q: A square screw has d<sub>m</sub> = 30 mm, lead 4 mm and μ = 0.12. Find the torque to raise 15 kN.
A nut must carry 50 kN on a thread with d<sub>m</sub> = 46 mm and depth 4 mm at 15 MPa. How many threads?
A screw with α = 5° and μ = 0.06 lowers its load by itself. Give two ways to make it hold the load.
quiz.a: tan 5° = 0.0875 > 0.06, so it overhauls. Reduce the lead (smaller α), or add collar friction or a brake: the lowering torque becomes (Wd<sub>m</sub>/2)tan(φ − α) + μ<sub>c</sub>WR<sub>m</sub>, which can be made positive.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ball screws replace sliding with rolling balls and reach efficiencies above 90 %, so CNC machine slides use them; they cannot self-lock and need a brake. Roller screws carry even higher loads in electric actuators. Search for ball screw preload and roller screw actuators.
